node.label: Glenda Elizabeth Gilmore
node.date_label: Gender and Jim Crow (1996) · Jumpin’ Jim Crow (coedited, 2000) · Defying Dixie (2008) · These United States (with Thomas J. Sugrue, 2015)
node.description: In Gender and Jim Crow (1996), Glenda Elizabeth Gilmore argued that educated Black women sustained political activism after Black men’s disfranchisement in North Carolina, using reform work and interracial contacts to exercise influence beyond electoral politics. Defying Dixie (2008) traced the radical, interracial and international struggles of 1919–1950 that preceded the better-known civil-rights movement. Gender and Jim Crow won the Frederick Jackson Turner Award and James A. Rawley Prize. Wali Rashash Kharif praised its recovery of Black women’s organizing but argued that it needed a fuller account of slavery’s legacy. David J. Garrow praised Defying Dixie’s treatment of white moderation while criticizing its speculation about earlier court-ordered desegregation and its allocation of responsibility for the Southern left’s defeat.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Gender and Jim Crow: Women and the Politics of White Supremacy in North Carolina, 1896–1920 (1996); Jumpin’ Jim Crow: Southern Politics from Civil War to Civil Rights, coedited with Jane Dailey and Bryant Simon (2000); Who Were the Progressives?, edited with an introduction (2002); Defying Dixie: The Radical Roots of Civil Rights, 1919–1950 (2008); These United States: A Nation in the Making, 1890 to the Present, with Thomas J. Sugrue (2015); Gender and Jim Crow, second edition with new author preface (2019).
node.scope_note: Major books and the 2011 Woodward essay were not read in full. Argument and reception claims rest on the publisher’s description, named scholarly reviews, Gilmore’s public interview excerpt and Yale’s institutional assessment. The original interview beyond the public opening is unread. Catalogue contents establish titles only.

proposed_edges.relationship: Gilmore credits Jacquelyn Dowd Hall, cochair of her dissertation committee for Gender and Jim Crow (dissertation 1992; book 1996), with encouraging history from below, labor analysis and attention to apparently lost causes.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: HNN interview excerpt, first question and answer (web lines 43–49): Gilmore states “Hall cochaired my dissertation committee” and describes the approach. CV p. 1 dates dissertation. Specific retrospective testimony; no sole-supervisor or sole-source claim. Original interview remainder and dissertation unread.
proposed_edges.map_label: Hall’s supervision and history from below

proposed_edges.relationship: Gilmore and Thomas J. Sugrue coauthored These United States: A Nation in the Making, 1890 to the Present (2015).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Sugrue’s own biography, paragraph beginning The Long Year (web lines 35–36), explicitly names the coauthor; Gilmore CV p. 2 dates trade book to 2015 and distinguishes 2016 textbooks. Collaboration only; no direction of intellectual dependence and no full-book reading.

proposed_edges.relationship: Gender and Jim Crow (1996) recovers Black women’s club, reform and interracial organizing as political action in North Carolina.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Kharif review, pp. 1–2, especially p. 2 paragraph beginning “Gilmore has carefully examined”: emphasizes club records and previously obscured female leadership. Complete review read; monograph unread. Regional and socially selective recovery, not a claim about all Southern women.

proposed_edges.relationship: Gender and Jim Crow (1996) explains how white-supremacist politics mobilized gender and how Black women developed political strategies within that racial order.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: UNC Press description of second edition, paragraphs 1–3 (web lines 72–75), especially “manipulation of concepts of gender.” Publisher summary read; 1996 original date checked in CV. Book and new preface unread; no direct derivation from Scott inferred.
proposed_edges.map_label: Gender and the making of white supremacy

proposed_edges.relationship: Defying Dixie (2008) extends the history of Black freedom struggles into interwar radical organizing and international connections.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: O’Brien review, opening paragraphs and final assessment (web lines 19–23, 40–41), singles out Soviet archival materials and struggles before 1955. Complete review read; book unread. Contribution is to historical scope and interpretation, not proof that every earlier organization directly produced later campaigns.
proposed_edges.map_label: Earlier radical roots of civil rights

proposed_edges.relationship: Gender and Jim Crow (1996) treats Black women's organizing after Black men's disfranchisement, including efforts to forge political ties with white women, as political activism.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: UNC Press description and quoted American Historical Review assessment (web lines 73–80), specifically “redefines what should count as” politics; Kharif pp. 1–2 corroborates organizing outside formal participation. Publisher page and complete Kharif review read, not the full AHR review or book. No general displacement of institutional political history claimed.

proposed_edges.relationship: Yale’s 2019 retirement tribute identifies the use of individual and family lives to build historical interpretation as a defining method in Gender and Jim Crow (1996) and Defying Dixie (2008).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Yale tribute, paragraphs 2–4 (web lines 72–74): describes “biography as the building blocks of historiography” and specifies Pettey’s family and the radical activists. Institutional methodological assessment; monographs unread. No claim that Gilmore founded collective biography.

proposed_edges.relationship: In the 2019 preface to Gender and Jim Crow (originally 1996), Gilmore credits Kimberlé Crenshaw’s critical race writing, identifying “Demarginalizing the Intersection of Race and Sex” (1989), with teaching her to recognize race in its stated absence and white supremacy as continually remade.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the publisher-linked licensed preview in its standard browser viewer, including the preface pp. xi–xvi. The body names Crenshaw and describes what her writing taught Gilmore; note 2 identifies the 1989 article. This is Gilmore’s retrospective intellectual-debt statement, not an inference from shared topics or a footnote. The underlying article and the complete 1996 book were not read for this backfill.

proposed_edges.relationship: Gilmore states in the 2019 preface to Gender and Jim Crow (originally 1996) that Robin D. G. Kelley’s Hammer and Hoe (1990) influenced her Defying Dixie (2008).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the publisher-linked licensed preview in its standard browser viewer, including the preface pp. xi–xvi. Gilmore directly names Kelley’s book and her own book in the influence sentence. Note 4 gives Hammer and Hoe’s original 1990 publication. Defying Dixie’s original 2008 year is retained from the supplied verified input. No broader claim of agreement or direct reading of either complete monograph is made.
proposed_edges.map_label: Hammer and Hoe influenced Defying Dixie

proposed_edges.relationship: In Defying Dixie: The Radical Roots of Civil Rights, 1919–1950 (2008), Gilmore connects southern struggles against racial segregation with Soviet communist networks and international antifascism, contributing a transnational account of the civil-rights movement’s radical precursors.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: O’Brien’s complete review was read. It identifies Soviet archives as an added resource and explains connections between southern activism and international movements. The global/connected-history classification is editorial, limited to these documented connections; the book itself remains unread.

verification.note: PDF pp. 1–4, education, honors, books and articles read; remaining pages only displayed in extraction. Supports titles, original years and editorial credits, not book arguments. The CV disagrees with the publisher on the new-preface edition year; publisher date retained.
